Jealous
JEL-us
adj.
From Old French jalous, from Late Latin zelosus, full of zeal, from Greek zelos. Webster 1828: suspicious that we do not enjoy the affection or respect of others; and, of God, solicitous for His own honour. The word is the same root as zeal, which is why Scripture can predicate it of God without any taint of pettiness.

Biblical Definition

God calls jealousy His name. Thou shalt worship no other god: for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God (Exodus 34:14). It is not an occasional mood but an attribute bound to His exclusive right to be worshipped, which is why it appears in the second commandment and in Moses’ warnings: the LORD thy God is a consuming fire, even a jealous God (Deuteronomy 4:24); the LORD thy God is a jealous God among you (Deuteronomy 6:15). Joshua presses it on a people making an easy profession: he is an holy God; he is a jealous God; he will not forgive your transgressions nor your sins (Joshua 24:19). The jealousy is also for His people’s good: Then will the LORD be jealous for his land, and pity his people (Joel 2:18), and He acts jealous for my holy name (Ezekiel 39:25). The marriage figure explains it. A husband’s jealousy over his wife is a covenant emotion, and Numbers 5 makes it a legal category. Paul takes the figure up without apology: I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2). Jealousy of that kind is the opposite of indifference.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines JEALOUS as suspicious of rivalry in love or honour; and, in the divine sense, solicitous to maintain one’s own honour and the purity of worship. He notes explicitly that God is jealous of His own glory and worship.

expand to see more

JEALOUS, a. — Suspicious; apprehensive of rivalship; uneasy through fear that another has withdrawn or may withdraw from one the affections of a person he loves.

Emulous; full of competition; zealous.

Solicitous to maintain or defend; as, jealous of one’s honour or reputation.

Applied to God, it denotes His solicitude for His own glory and the purity of His worship — the LORD, whose name is Jealous.

Webster’s progression is the theological answer to the modern objection. Human jealousy is corrupted by insecurity; divine jealousy is the zeal of a Husband with an absolute right, which no rival can either threaten or deserve.

Key Scripture

Exodus 34:14 — "For thou shalt worship no other god: for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God:"

Deuteronomy 4:24 — "For the LORD thy God is a consuming fire, even a jealous God."

Joshua 24:19 — "And Joshua said unto the people, Ye cannot serve the LORD: for he is an holy God; he is a jealous God; he will not forgive your transgressions nor your sins."

Joel 2:18 — "Then will the LORD be jealous for his land, and pity his people."

2 Corinthians 11:2 — "For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ."

Modern Corruption

Divine jealousy is corrupted when it is read through human insecurity — as though God were petty or possessive — and it is quietly deleted whenever the second commandment is treated as a comment on ancient idols rather than as a live claim on worship.

expand to see more

The standard objection says that jealousy is a vice, and a jealous God is therefore an unworthy one. It rests on a confusion. Human jealousy is usually sinful because it is either envy of what another rightly has, or a suspicion born of insecurity about a claim we do not actually possess. Neither applies to God. He has an absolute right to the worship of His creatures, and no rival has any claim on it at all. The husband analogy Paul uses in 2 Corinthians 11:2 makes the point: a husband indifferent to his wife’s adultery is not admirably tolerant, he is a man who does not love her. Divine jealousy is the necessary form love takes when the covenant is exclusive and it is being violated.

The quieter corruption is practical. Exodus 34:14 states the jealousy as the ground of a prohibition on other gods, and the second commandment attaches it to images. Where worship is arranged according to what moves an audience rather than what God has commanded, the jealousy has not been argued away but simply ignored. Joshua 24:19 is the sobering case: a congregation making an enthusiastic profession is told Ye cannot serve the LORD, because the God they were volunteering to serve is holy and jealous. Joshua was not discouraging them from covenant; he was insisting they count the cost of one. And the same jealousy is their hope, since a God jealous for His holy name will not let His people go.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew qanna' is used only of God and describes His zeal for His exclusive covenant right; the related noun covers both the husband’s jealousy of Numbers 5 and God’s. The Greek zelos gives English both zeal and jealousy.

expand to see more

Hebrew qanna' (H7067) — jealous; used in Scripture only of God (Exodus 34:14; Deuteronomy 4:24; 6:15; Joshua 24:19).

Hebrew qin'ah (H7068) — jealousy, zeal, ardour; the spirit of jealousy in the law of Numbers 5 and the LORD’s zeal for His land in Joel 2:18.

Hebrew El Qanna' — a jealous God, a divine title attached to the second commandment (Exodus 20:5).

Greek zelos (G2205) — zeal or jealousy according to context; I am jealous over you with godly jealousy (2 Corinthians 11:2).

The single Greek root behind English zeal and jealousy explains why Scripture can predicate the affection of God without predicating the vice.

Usage

"The LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God (Exodus 34:14) — jealousy stated as a name, not a mood."

"He is an holy God; he is a jealous God (Joshua 24:19) — spoken to a congregation making a cheap profession."

"I am jealous over you with godly jealousy (2 Corinthians 11:2) — the pastor’s duty to guard a betrothed church."
